newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Fed comments take center stage.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Fed comments take center stage.

text.p: The monthly U.S. trade report, which in the late 1980s riveted the financial markets' attention, is likely to take a back seat to remarks of various Federal Reserve officials on Wednesday, analysts said.

The U.S. Treasury market returned to a highly anxious state on Tuesday, worrying again that the Fed was leaning toward raising interest rates at its September 24 policy meeting. Last week, the market's fears of higher rates had been soothed by benign inflation data and especially by news of a very slight increase in August retail sales.
At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday, the Commerce Department will report July U.S. trade figures.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast an $8.8 billion August trade gap versus an $8.1 July shortfall. Renewed domestic demand for imported goods and a recent runup in oil prices widened the deficit, they said.
Sandy Batten, international economist at Citicorp Global Finance, said the trade data might possibly affect the dollar, but not the credit markets.

Batten said Reuters' report on Tuesday that eight of 12 Fed banks have submitted requests for a discount rate hike and that the consensus centers around a 25-basis-point hike on September 24 had heightened the market's sensitivity to any comments Fed officials might make on Wednesday.

Two Fed officials are officially set to make public remarks on Wednesday. Fed Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin will address an Institute of International Bankers luncheon scheduled for 1200 EDT/1600 GMT in New York.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, Fed Gov. Susan Phillips is scheduled to testify before the House Banking Committee.
Meanwhile, a conference on international trade hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago will continue in Chicago.
And the market will be well aware of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's planned appearance at a U.S. Treasury conference on electronic money and banking on Thursday evening.
"I really don't think trade is going to be a major market mover," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Instead, the market is likely to be preoccupied with the Fed's next policy decision, he said.
"Unexpected comments from Fed officials, given the market's anxiety about a tightening, that's what creates (some volatility)," said Flanagan.
Flanagan said the uncertainty about a potential Fed tightening move "will probably stay with us until Tuesday" when Fed policy makers meet.

"There's less conviction about what the Fed will do this time and the stories (from Fed sources and officials) are adding to the uncertainty. That creates some anxiety within the market's pricing mechanism," he said.

James Glassman, economist at Chase Securities, said in his view, the September 24 meeting would be the best time for the Fed to tighten a small amount because the markets are in a position to cope with a small rate hike.

"If they tighten now, it looks like a little insurance," he said. "It looks like the Fed isn't behind if they go now. That's the beauty of it. Inflation isn't a big risk now but the prudent thing for a central bank is to not take risks."
Fed funds, trading at a soft 4-3/4 percent late Tuesday, should open at 5-3/16 percent on Wednesday, dealers said.
The 30-year bond yield was down 30/32 to 96-18/32, yielding 7.03 percent in late trade on Tuesday.
